name: Schwarzschild Black Hole in a Tidal Field
description: Schwarzschild's black hole in the quadrupole field of distant matter, a static vacuum solution of Weyl's class that A. G. Doroshkevich, Yakov Zel'dovich, and Igor Novikov gave in 1965, and the simplest of the distorted black holes of Robert Geroch and James Hartle. The tidal field flattens or stretches the horizon and leaves it regular; it grows with distance, so the solution holds between the horizon and the matter that distorts it.
convention: The mass parameter $m = GM/c^2$ is a length and the quadrupole parameter $q$ is a pure number. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A black hole in the sky keeps company: a disc of gas around it, or a partner star in orbit [gurlebeck2015]. Karl Schwarzschild's solution of 1916 has room for neither, since it is the field of one round mass with nothing else in the universe [schwarzschild1916]. Werner Israel proved in 1967 that a static black hole left alone, in a vacuum that flattens out far away, can only be Schwarzschild's [israel1967, frolovshoom2007]. So what becomes of the horizon when the neighbours pull on it?¶A. G. Doroshkevich, Yakov Zel'dovich, and Igor Novikov had an answer in print two years before the theorem [doroshkevich1965, israel1967]. In a paper on stars that collapse out of round, submitted on 16 December 1964, they showed with Erez and Rosen's metric that a quadrupole of the star's own turns the horizon into a naked singularity [doroshkevich1965]. In its fourth appendix they put the quadrupole outside, and gave the exact field of "a spherical mass $m$ in an external quadrupole field (which increases with increasing distance from the mass $m$)" [doroshkevich1965]. There the surface $g_{tt} = 0$ "is a Schwarzschild sphere deformed by the external fields, with all its properties" [doroshkevich1965]. They said who does the pulling, too: "remote masses which are secured to supports that prevent their displacement" [doroshkevich1965].¶The recipe is Hermann Weyl's, from 1917, and it turns the vacuum around a static body with an axis into a problem from Newton's theory [weyl1917]. Einstein's equations leave a potential that solves Laplace's equation of flat space, and since that equation is linear, the potential of the distant masses adds to Schwarzschild's [weyl1917, fairhurst2001]. Laplace's equation has two quadrupole solutions: one dies away with distance and belongs to the body, and the other grows with distance and belongs to whatever lies outside [shoom2016]. Erez and Rosen's metric takes the first and the appendix of Doroshkevich, Zel'dovich, and Novikov the second, $\psi = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\frac{x - 1}{x + 1} + \tfrac{q}{4}\left(3x^2 - 1\right)\left(3y^2 - 1\right)$ in the prolate spheroidal coordinates $x$ and $y$ [doroshkevich1965, frolovshoom2007].¶The general case, any gravitational field laid over Schwarzschild's, is Lawrence Mysak and George Szekeres's of 1966 [mysak1966]. Static disturbances, they found, "generally have no effect on the nature of the singularity", while "time-dependent disturbances of an assumed form convert it from a coordinate singularity into a true, coordinate-independent singularity" [mysak1966]. The singularity of their title is the surface $r = 2m$, the horizon [mysak1966]. By 1982 Robert Geroch and James Hartle had the whole static family: "All exact solutions of Einstein's equation that represent static, axisymmetric black holes distorted by an external matter distribution are obtained" [geroch1982]. Any potential will do that is smooth on the horizon and takes one value at its two poles [frolovshoom2007]. Israel's proof needs a field that flattens out far away, and this one grows with distance, so the solution describes the neighbourhood of the hole, inside the matter that does the pulling [israel1967, fairhurst2001].¶Geroch and Hartle took the hole's temperature as well, and gave it laws of thermodynamics [geroch1982]. The surface gravity, which sets that temperature, is one number over the whole bent horizon, $e^{2q}/4m$ in units of $c^2$, and the mass measured on the horizon is still $m$ [frolovshoom2007, fairhurst2001]. Valeri Frolov and Andrey Shoom found the shape in 2007: a ring of matter around the equator, $q > 0$, flattens the horizon, and masses on the axis, $q < 0$, stretch it [frolovshoom2007]. Past $q = 1/12$ the Gaussian curvature of the horizon "becomes negative at both of the poles", and the surface "cannot be isometrically embedded in a flat 3D space" [frolovshoom2007]. They followed the potential inside the horizon too, where its value next to the singularity is fixed by its value on the horizon [frolovshoom2007].¶A star in a tidal field grows a bulge, a quadrupole moment of its own, and its Love number says how large [binnington2009]. Does a black hole grow one? The relativistic answer came in 2009 from Taylor Binnington and Eric Poisson: "the relativistic Love numbers of a nonrotating black hole are all zero" [binnington2009]. Norman Gürlebeck proved it in 2015 without approximation, for Geroch and Hartle's holes: the tidal field induces no multipole moment in the hole, which "still has no hair" [gurlebeck2015]. So a black hole with a quadrupole of its own loses its horizon, as Erez and Rosen's metric shows, and a quadrupole pressed on it from outside bends the horizon and raises none in reply [doroshkevich1965, gurlebeck2015]. When Shohreh Abdolrahimi, Robert Mann, and Christos Tzounis traced light past the hole in 2015, they found "that a prolate distortion of the horizon gives rise to an oblate distortion of the shadow, and vice-versa" [abdolrahimi2015].

related.text: The hole with nobody near, $q = 0$. Among static black holes in a vacuum that flattens out far away it is the only one [israel1967].

The same recipe with the other quadrupole, the one that dies away with distance and belongs to the body itself. That one turns the horizon into a naked singularity for every $q \neq 0$ [doroshkevich1965].

Another deformation of Schwarzschild's rod in Weyl's class, which changes the density of the rod. It too puts a naked singularity where the horizon was, as a deformation of the body itself does [shoom2016].
Ernst's black hole in Melvin's magnetic universe is the same idea with a magnetic field for the surroundings: a regular horizon in a field that never flattens out [fairhurst2001].
A black hole pulled along its axis by a string or pushed by a strut, static and axisymmetric as well. Its horizon carries a conical singularity where the string meets it [fairhurst2001].
Another member of Weyl's class, built on the Newtonian potential of a point. Here the potential is that of Schwarzschild's rod plus a quadrupole that grows with distance [bicak2000, frolovshoom2007].

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass of the black hole

Quadrupole parameter of the external field, a pure number; $q > 0$ flattens the horizon, as a ring of matter in the equatorial plane does, $q < 0$ stretches it along the axis, as masses on the axis do, and $q = 0$ is Schwarzschild's metric

The potential of the distant matter, the quadrupole harmonic that is regular on the horizon and grows with distance; it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_x\left(\left(x^2 - 1\right)\partial_xU\right) + \partial_y\left(\left(1 - y^2\right)\partial_yU\right) = 0$

Fixed by $U$ through $\partial_xV = \dfrac{1 - y^2}{x^2 - y^2}\left(x\left(x^2 - 1\right)\left(\partial_xU\right)^2 - x\left(1 - y^2\right)\left(\partial_yU\right)^2 - 2y\left(x^2 - 1\right)\partial_xU\,\partial_yU + 2x\,\partial_xU - 2y\,\partial_yU\right)$ and $\partial_yV = \dfrac{1}{x^2 - y^2}\left(\left(x^2 - 1\right)\left(y\left(x^2 - 1\right)\left(\partial_xU\right)^2 - y\left(1 - y^2\right)\left(\partial_yU\right)^2 + 2x\left(1 - y^2\right)\partial_xU\,\partial_yU + 2y\,\partial_xU\right) + 2x\left(1 - y^2\right)\partial_yU\right)$, zero on the axis $y = \pm 1$, and equal to $2U - 2q$ on the horizon

coordinates.convention: We use prolate spheroidal coordinates $(t, x, y, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $x$ and $y$ pure numbers; Weyl's canonical coordinates are $\rho = m\sqrt{(x^2 - 1)(1 - y^2)}$ and $z = mxy$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

parameters.description: Mass parameter, a length, $m = GM/c^2$ with $M$ the mass of the black hole

Quadrupole parameter of the external field, a pure number; $q > 0$ flattens the horizon, as a ring of matter in the equatorial plane does, $q < 0$ stretches it along the axis, as masses on the axis do, and $q = 0$ is Schwarzschild's metric

The potential of the distant matter, the quadrupole harmonic that is regular on the horizon and grows with distance; it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_r\left(\left(r^2 - 2mr\right)\partial_rU\right) + \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta\left(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta U\right) = 0$

Fixed by $U$ through $\partial_rV = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{r^2 - 2mr + m^2\sin^2\theta}\left(\left(r - m\right)\sin\theta\left(\left(r^2 - 2mr\right)\left(\partial_rU\right)^2 - \left(\partial_\theta U\right)^2 + 2m\,\partial_rU\right) + 2\cos\theta\left(\left(r^2 - 2mr\right)\partial_rU + m\right)\partial_\theta U\right)$ and $\partial_\theta V = -\dfrac{\sin\theta}{r^2 - 2mr + m^2\sin^2\theta}\left(\left(r^2 - 2mr\right)\cos\theta\left(\left(r^2 - 2mr\right)\left(\partial_rU\right)^2 - \left(\partial_\theta U\right)^2 + 2m\,\partial_rU\right) - 2\left(r - m\right)\sin\theta\left(\left(r^2 - 2mr\right)\partial_rU + m\right)\partial_\theta U\right)$, zero on the axis $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = \pi$, and equal to $2U - 2q$ on the horizon

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ that are Schwarzschild's at $q = 0$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ a length. The prolate spheroidal coordinates are $x = r/m - 1$ and $y = \cos\theta$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.convention: We use Weyl's canonical coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ and $z$ lengths; the horizon is the rod $\rho = 0$, $|z| \le m$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
